paper.abstract: Abstract Airy beams are often proposed in array beamforming to bend beams around obstacles. We prove that, for a single-antenna receiver, conventional beamfocusing maximizes the received power regardless of how many antennas are blocked and, in expectation, even with phase errors in the channel state information. This also holds for multi-antenna receivers under a phase-separability condition that is satisfied in rank-one channels. Numerical results confirm that unmodified beamfocusing is optimal for physically small receivers (i.e., those that fit within the beamwidth) when an obstacle is present. For physically larger receivers, the optimal precoding deviates from beamfocusing to better illuminate the receiver’s unobstructed parts, but will not become Airy beams. While Airy beams can be configured to perform well, their ability to follow a bent trajectory in front of an obstacle does not maximize the received power behind it.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: The radiative near-field of an antenna array is the region where it must consider the nonlinear wavefront curvature when transmitting to a receiver, even if the receiver is in the far-field of the individual antenna elements [ 1 , 2 ] . This regime is particularly relevant to millimeter-wave (mmWave) and terahertz (THz) systems, where short wavelengths and electrically large apertures with very many antennas may place most users in the near field [ 2 , 3 ] . In a single-user link with known channel coefficients, maximum-ratio transmission (MRT) maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) subject to a total-power constraint [ 4 ] . In line-of-sight (LOS) scenarios, its phase shifts compensate for the individual path distances, producing beamfocusing with limited depth in the near field, rather than only steering in an angular direction [ 1 ] . Analog precoding, typical to mmWave and THz systems, retains this phase compensation but uses equal power per antenna. Wavefront engineering refers to actively shaping the spatial evolution of the transmitted field, especially in the near-field, by controlling phase and amplitude over the transmitting array [ 3 ] . Examples include Bessel beams, proposed for extended depth of focus (compared to beamfocusing) and self-healing after partial obstruction [ 3 , 5 ] , and Airy beams, associated with curved mainlobe trajectories and self-healing [ 6 ] . These features can only be partially realized with finite-sized apertures and hardware constraints (e.g., analog precoding), but a closed-form phase-only Airy-beam design was recently developed in [ 7 ] . Blockage provides a prominent motivation for these self-healing beam designs and is a practical issue in mmWave/THz systems [ 4 ] . We use quasi-LOS to describe LOS links where an object obstructs the direct paths from some transmit antennas to the receiver while leaving others unaffected. Airy beams have been particularly proposed for enhancing connectivity in these scenarios, with claims that they “ realize a link by curving around an intervening obstacle ” [ 8 ] and “ curve around the LOS obstruction and deliver maximum power to the receiver ” [ 9 ] . However, the usefulness of Airy beams in such scenarios was challenged in [ 10 ] , concluding that the “ beamfocusing strategy already attains near-optimal performance ”. These developments motivate the research question addressed in this paper: When is it desirable to switch from beamfocusing to other beams (e.g., Airy) in the presence of a partially blocking object? We investigate this question for quasi-LOS links with analog phase-only precoding and an explicit analytically tractable antenna-attenuation model. We characterize the SNR-maximizing precoding with and without phase uncertainty at the transmitter, examine extensions to multiple receive antennas, and relate Airy-beam phase profiles to their curved spatial trajectories. The results provide a precise answer to the question under specific conditions. Simulations are used to compare beamfocusing and Airy beams to corroborate the analytical results, explore their generality, and provide further insights into the key properties of these beam types.

sections.heading: V Beamfocusing Versus Airy Beams
sections.text: Precoding that generates Airy beams has been described as suitable for quasi-LOS scenarios because it has a mainlobe with a bent locus, in contrast to the ellipsoidal mainlobe of beamfocusing. Recall that the m m :th antenna has coordinate x m x_{m} along the x x -axis. We now let z > 0 z>0 denote the coordinate in the perpendicular direction. Such a change might, however, modify the beam shape around the receiver, as studied next. Fig. 1 shows the results of a numerical example adapted from [ 7 , Fig. 3] , in which a ULA with M = 256 M=256 antennas and Δ = λ / 2 \Delta=\lambda/2 is used at 140 140 GHz. The aperture length is 27 27 cm. The multiple antennas and beam shaping result in a power gain that we calculate at each location by dividing the actual received power by what it would have been with a single antenna at the origin. The value is shown in dB-scale relative to the theoretical maximum, so that 0 0 dB represents M = 256 M=256 . Fig. 1a shows the power gain pattern of a transmitted Airy beam with B = 5 B=5 m -1 , F = 0.5 F=0.5 m, and ϑ = − 0.03 \vartheta=-0.03 rad. The array is indicated as a red line along the vertical axis, and the approximate trajectory curve from ( 26 ) is shown as a dashed curve that roughly follows the actual beam locus. Next, Fig. 1b shows the power gain pattern when an object (shown in orange) is placed in front of the lower half of the array at a distance of 0.66 0.66 m and lets no signal through (i.e., d m = 0 d_{m}=0 for affected antennas). The mainlobe is barely affected (the Airy configuration was selected to enable this), but a region behind the object cannot be reached at all, and there is also slightly less power gain in some of the upper sidelobes. Suppose the intended receiver is located at the red circle, which is z = 2.5 z=2.5 m from the array and placed on the trajectory curve with x A ​ ( 2.5 ) ≈ − 0.05 x_{\mathrm{A}}(2.5)\approx-0.05 m. If our goal is to maximize the SNR at this receiver, we could instead use beamfocusing configured for this location. The resulting beam pattern is shown in Fig. 1c . When the blockage is present, the lower half of the array cannot reach the receiver, so the beam pattern is distorted into the one shown in Fig. 1d . Interestingly, in the presence of the blocking object, Airy and beamfocusing achieve visually similar beam shapes around the receiver, while the main differences are elsewhere. Simply put, the Airy beam uses antennas that cannot reach the receiver to create the curved part of the main lobe in front of the object—the beam does not bend around the object but bends before it. The power gain at the receiver is 256 256 ( 0 0 dB) with beamfocusing and 39 39 ( − 8.1 -8.1 dB) with the Airy beam in the absence of blockage. It drops to 49 49 ( − 7.2 -7.2 dB) and 38 38 ( − 8.2 -8.2 dB), respectively, under blockage. Hence, beamfocusing remains the preferable precoding even when there is a blocking object, as proved by Lemma 1 . Only 112 112 of the 256 256 antennas have an unobstructed view of the receiver, so when using beamfocusing, we lose both the blocked antennas’ power and contribution to the array gain. This explains why the power gain becomes 256 ⋅ ( 112 256 ) 2 = 49 256\cdot(\frac{112}{256})^{2}=49 . By contrast, the power gain of the Airy beam is barely affected by the object, as it spreads its power along a curved trajectory. However, the peak gain is only 15 15 % of that with beamfocusing (without blockage).

The SNR generally increases with the number of receive antennas. sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we examined whether using Airy beams at the transmitter can outperform conventional focused beams in mitigating partial blockage in near-field quasi-LOS communications. Under our modeling assumptions, we mathematically and numerically illustrated that the same beamfocusing-type precoder achieves the highest SNR in quasi-LOS channels for both single-antenna and small-scale multi-antenna receivers (rank-one channel), as well as for both certain and uncertain channel models. The transmitter can even be unaware of the blockage. We further noticed that the bending property of the Airy beam family allows us to tailor its trajectory to a specific obstacle, thereby achieving an almost “blockage-agnostic” configuration with a similar beam pattern with and without that obstacle. Yet, Airy beams are not optimal in terms of the SNR achieved at a receiver behind the obstacle. The suboptimal performance of bent Airy beams was shown for both small-scale receivers, where they are inferior to beamfocusing, and receivers larger than the beamwidth. In the latter case, they are outperformed by joint precoder/combiner optimization, which focuses signals on the unobstructed parts of the receiver.

Larsson 2 Affiliation: 1 Department of Communication Systems, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden, {emilbjo,vitalyp}@kth.se Affiliation: 2 Dept. of Electrical Engineering (ISY), Linköping University, Linköping, Sweden, erik.g.larsson@liu.se Affiliation: Abstract Airy beams are often proposed in array beamforming to bend beams around obstacles. We prove that, for a single-antenna receiver, conventional beamfocusing maximizes the received power regardless of how many antennas are blocked and, in expectation, even with phase errors in the channel state information. This also holds for multi-antenna receivers under a phase-separability condition that is satisfied in rank-one channels. Numerical results confirm that unmodified beamfocusing is optimal for physically small receivers (i.e., those that fit within the beamwidth) when an obstacle is present. For physically larger receivers, the optimal precoding deviates from beamfocusing to better illuminate the receiver’s unobstructed parts, but will not become Airy beams. While Airy beams can be configured to perform well, their ability to follow a bent trajectory in front of an obstacle does not maximize the received power behind it. Index Terms: Beamfocusing, Airy beams, wavefront engineering, partial blockages, mmWave, THz, phase uncertainty. I Introduction The radiative near-field of an antenna array is the region where it must consider the nonlinear wavefront curvature when transmitting to a receiver, even if the receiver is in the far-field of the individual antenna elements [ 1 , 2 ] . This regime is particularly relevant to millimeter-wave (mmWave) and terahertz (THz) systems, where short wavelengths and electrically large apertures with very many antennas may place most users in the near field [ 2 , 3 ] . In a single-user link with known channel coefficients, maximum-ratio transmission (MRT) maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) subject to a total-power constraint [ 4 ] . In line-of-sight (LOS) scenarios, its phase shifts compensate for the individual path distances, producing beamfocusing with limited depth in the near field, rather than only steering in an angular direction [ 1 ] . Analog precoding, typical to mmWave and THz systems, retains this phase compensation but uses equal power per antenna. Wavefront engineering refers to actively shaping the spatial evolution of the transmitted field, especially in the near-field, by controlling phase and amplitude over the transmitting array [ 3 ] . Examples include Bessel beams, proposed for extended depth of focus (compared to beamfocusing) and self-healing after partial obstruction [ 3 , 5 ] , and Airy beams, associated with curved mainlobe trajectories and self-healing [ 6 ] . These features can only be partially realized with finite-sized apertures and hardware constraints (e.g., analog precoding), but a closed-form phase-only Airy-beam design was recently developed in [ 7 ] . Blockage provides a prominent motivation for these self-healing beam designs and is a practical issue in mmWave/THz systems [ 4 ] . We use quasi-LOS to describe LOS links where an object obstructs the direct paths from some transmit antennas to the receiver while leaving others unaffected. Airy beams have been particularly proposed for enhancing connectivity in these scenarios, with claims that they “ realize a link by curving around an intervening obstacle ” [ 8 ] and “ curve around the LOS obstruction and deliver maximum power to the receiver ” [ 9 ] . However, the usefulness of Airy beams in such scenarios was challenged in [ 10 ] , concluding that the “ beamfocusing strategy already attains near-optimal performance ”. These developments motivate the research question addressed in this paper: When is it desirable to switch from beamfocusing to other beams (e.g., Airy) in the presence of a partially blocking object? We investigate this question for quasi-LOS links with analog phase-only precoding and an explicit analytically tractable antenna-attenuation model. We characterize the SNR-maximizing precoding with and without phase uncertainty at the transmitter, examine extensions to multiple receive antennas, and relate Airy-beam phase profiles to their curved spatial trajectories. The results provide a precise answer to the question under specific conditions. Simulations are used to compare beamfocusing and Airy beams to corroborate the analytical results, explore their generality, and provide further insights into the key properties of these beam types. VI Conclusion In this paper, we examined whether using Airy beams at the transmitter can outperform conventional focused beams in mitigating partial blockage in near-field quasi-LOS communications. Under our modeling assumptions, we mathematically and numerically illustrated that the same beamfocusing-type precoder achieves the highest SNR in quasi-LOS channels for both single-antenna and small-scale multi-antenna receivers (rank-one channel), as well as for both certain and uncertain channel models. The transmitter can even be unaware of the blockage. We further noticed that the bending property of the Airy beam family allows us to tailor its trajectory to a specific obstacle, thereby achieving an almost “blockage-agnostic” configuration with a similar beam pattern with and without that obstacle. Yet, Airy beams are not optimal in terms of the SNR achieved at a receiver behind the obstacle. The suboptimal performance of bent Airy beams was shown for both small-scale receivers, where they are inferior to beamfocusing, and receivers larger than the beamwidth.
